rewritten_text:
They were bringing along a very respectable-looking old gentleman and a pleasant-looking younger man whose right arm was in a sling. Goodness, how the crowd shouted and laughed! They kept it up, too. I couldn't see anything funny, and I guessed the duke and king would have trouble finding the joke themselves. I expected them to turn pale. But neither one lost a bit of colour. The duke gave no sign that he suspected what was happening. He just went on making contented noises, like a jug gurgling out buttermilk. As for the king, he stared down at the newcomers with such sorrow that you'd think the existence of frauds and scoundrels gave him a stomachache right in his heart. Oh, he did it beautifully. Plenty of the town's leading people gathered around him to show their support. The old gentleman who had just arrived looked utterly confused. Before long he began speaking, and I noticed immediately that he sounded English—different from the king, though the king's imitation was pretty good. I can't remember his exact words or copy his accent, but he turned to the crowd and said something like this:

‘This is an unexpected surprise, and I'll admit frankly that I'm poorly equipped to deal with it or defend myself. My brother and I have had some bad luck. He's broken his arm, and last night our luggage was mistakenly unloaded at a town upriver. I am Peter Wilks's brother Harvey. This is his brother William, who cannot hear or speak. He can barely even communicate by signs now, with only one hand available. We are exactly who we say we are. Once I get our luggage in a day or two, I can prove it. Until then, I'll say no more, but go to the hotel and wait.’

He and the other deaf man began to leave. The king laughed and called out:

‘A broken arm—how very believable! And wonderfully convenient for an impostor who needs to use sign language but hasn't learned it. Lost their luggage! That's excellent! Very clever indeed, under the circumstances!’

He laughed again, and everyone joined in except three or four people, or perhaps half a dozen. One was the doctor. Another was a sharp-looking gentleman carrying an old-fashioned travelling bag made from carpet material. He had just left the steamboat and was speaking quietly with the doctor. They glanced toward the king now and then and nodded to each other. This was Levi Bell, the lawyer who had gone to Louisville. Another person who wasn't laughing was a big, rough, powerful fellow. He had come up and listened to everything the old gentleman said, and now he was listening to the king.

Even now I had not swallowed the last bitter drops of my suffering. I had not fully accepted my loss. I did not yet feel with every heartbeat, every nerve, every thought, that I alone remained of the human race—that I was the LAST MAN.

Clouds had gathered during the day, and at sunset a light rain began. Even the everlasting sky is weeping, I thought. Why should a mortal man be ashamed to exhaust himself in tears? I remembered the old legends in which people wept until they dissolved into endlessly flowing springs. If only that could happen to me! Then my fate would resemble, in some way, the deaths of Adrian and Clara in the water. Oh, grief has a strange imagination. From every shape and change around it, it spins a web on which to write the story of its suffering. It joins itself to all living nature and feeds on every object. Like light, it fills everything; like light, it gives everything its own colours.

My search had taken me some distance from the place where I had washed ashore. I came upon one of the watchtowers built at regular intervals along the Italian coast. I welcomed the shelter and the sight of something made by human hands, after looking so long at nature's bleak emptiness. I entered and climbed the rough spiral staircase to the guardroom. Fate was kind enough to spare me any distressing remains of the people who had once lived there. A few boards resting on two iron stands, covered in dry corn leaves, offered a bed. An open chest held some partly mouldy biscuits. Seeing them woke my appetite; perhaps I had been hungry already, but until then I had not noticed. I also suffered a fierce, burning thirst from exhaustion and the seawater I had swallowed. Nature kindly makes the relief of these needs pleasurable. So even I—even I!—felt refreshed and soothed as I ate that miserable food and drank a little sour wine from a half-full flask left in the deserted tower. Then I lay down on the bed, which no shipwreck survivor would have rejected. After the hateful smell of seaweed, the earthy scent of the dried leaves comforted me. I forgot that I was alone. I thought neither of the past nor of the future. My senses grew quiet, and I fell asleep. I dreamed of beloved places inland, of people making hay, and of a shepherd whistling for his dog to help bring the flock into its pen. I dreamed of sights and sounds from my mountain childhood that I had long forgotten.

‘Good heavens!’ the Duchess thought. ‘He is some sort of foot doctor after all. How dreadful. I hope at least he's a foreigner. That would make it slightly less awful.’

‘I simply must introduce you to him.’

‘Introduce me!’ cried the Duchess. ‘Surely you don't mean he's here?’ She began searching for her little tortoiseshell fan and badly frayed lace shawl, preparing to leave at a moment's notice.

‘Of course he's here. I wouldn't dream of hosting a party without him. He says I have a purely psychic hand, and that if my thumb were even slightly shorter, I'd have become a hopeless pessimist and entered a convent.’

‘Oh, I understand!’ said the Duchess, greatly relieved. ‘He tells fortunes, I suppose?’

‘Misfortunes too,’ Lady Windermere replied. ‘Any number of them. Next year, for example, I'll be in terrible danger on both land and sea, so I intend to live in a balloon and have my dinner pulled up in a basket every evening. It's all written on my little finger, or the palm of my hand—I forget which.’

‘But surely that's tempting Providence, Gladys.’

‘My dear Duchess, Providence ought to be able to resist temptation by now. I think everyone should have their palms read once a month to learn what they shouldn't do. Of course they do it anyway, but being warned is so pleasant. Now, unless someone fetches Mr. Podgers immediately, I shall have to go myself.’

‘Let me find him, Lady Windermere,’ said a tall, handsome young man who had been standing nearby, listening with an amused smile.

‘Thank you so much, Lord Arthur, but I'm afraid you wouldn't recognize him.’

‘If he's as remarkable as you say, Lady Windermere, I can hardly miss him. Describe him to me and I'll bring him straight over.’

‘Well, he doesn't look remotely like a palm reader. I mean, there's nothing mysterious, mystical, or romantic about his appearance. He's short and stout, with a funny bald head and enormous gold-rimmed glasses. Somewhere between a family doctor and a provincial lawyer. I'm terribly sorry, but it isn't my fault. People can be so irritating. Every one of my pianists looks exactly like a poet, and all my poets look exactly like pianists. Last season, I remember, I invited a most dreadful conspirator to dinner. He had blown up any number of people, always wore chain mail, and kept a dagger up his shirt sleeve. And do you know, when he arrived he looked just like a kindly old clergyman and spent the entire evening telling jokes?’
